content: The longissimus muscle is located lateral to the semispinalis muscle. It is the longest subdivision of the sacrospinalis muscle group and extends forward into the transverse processes of the posterior cervical vertebrae. The longissimus dorsi is the intermediate and largest continuation of the sacrospinalis muscle. In the lumbar region, where it is still blended with the iliocostalis lumborum, some of its fibers attach to the entire length of the posterior surfaces of the transverse processes and accessory processes of the lumbar vertebrae, as well as to the anterior layer of the lumbodorsal fascia. In the thoracic region, it inserts via rounded tendons into the tips of the transverse processes of all thoracic vertebrae and via fleshy processes into the lower nine or ten ribs, specifically between their tubercles and angles. The longissimus cervicis, also known as the transversalis cervicis, is positioned medial to the longissimus dorsi. It originates via long, thin tendons from the summits of the transverse processes of the upper four or five thoracic vertebrae. It inserts via similar tendons into the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, spanning from the second to the sixth vertebrae inclusively. The longissimus capitis, also referred to as the trachelomastoid muscle, lies medial to the longissimus cervicis, situated between it and the semispinalis capitis. It originates via tendons from the transverse processes of the upper four or five thoracic vertebrae and the articular processes of the lower three or four cervical vertebrae. It inserts into the posterior margin of the mastoid process, beneath the splenius capitis and sternocleidomastoideus muscles. This muscle is almost always crossed by a tendinous intersection near its insertion.
